query_text: what causes your bladder not to empty

action.query: Mayo Clinic urinary retention causes bladder doesn't empty completely
queries: Mayo Clinic urinary retention causes bladder doesn't empty completely
NIDDK urinary retention causes incomplete bladder emptying

content.text:
A bladder that doesn’t empty fully is called **urinary retention**. It usually happens for one of two broad reasons: **something is blocking urine from leaving**, or **the bladder muscle/nerve signals aren’t working well enough to push urine out**. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))

Common causes include:

- **Enlarged prostate** in men, which can squeeze the urethra and slow or block urine flow.
- **Urethral stricture** — narrowing/scarring of the tube urine passes through.
- **Bladder stones, kidney/ureter stones, blood clots, tumors**, or other blockages.
- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)** or inflammation causing swelling and difficulty urinating.
- **Constipation**, which can press on the bladder/urethra or affect pelvic nerves.
- **Nerve problems** from diabetes, stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, or pelvic surgery.
- **Medications**, especially some antihistamines, decongestants, antidepressants, sedatives, muscle relaxers, opioids, and some bladder-control medicines.
- **Pelvic organ prolapse** in women, where the bladder/uterus/rectum drops and kinks or obstructs urine flow.
- **Weak bladder muscle**, sometimes from aging, chronic over-distention, diabetes, or nerve damage.
- **After surgery/anesthesia**, urinary retention can happen temporarily. ([my.clevelandclinic.org](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15427-urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))

**Seek urgent medical care now** if you **can’t pee at all**, have severe lower belly pain/bloating, fever, back/flank pain, vomiting, new leg weakness/numbness, or blood clots in the urine. Acute urinary retention is considered a medical emergency because pressure can back up and harm the bladder or kidneys. ([my.clevelandclinic.org](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15427-urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))

If this is ongoing but not an emergency, it’s still worth seeing a clinician/urologist. They can check a urine test, kidney function, prostate/pelvic exam, and measure “post-void residual” urine with an ultrasound to see how much is left after you pee.
